title: After a hip replacement: coming home when you are frail (UK)
meta_title: Coming Home After Hip Replacement When You Are Frail
meta_description: What to expect in the first weeks at home after a hip replacement if you are frail: exercises, equipment, pain relief, warning signs and support.
excerpt: What to expect in the first weeks at home after a hip replacement if you are frail: exercises, equipment, pain relief, warning signs and support.
direct_answer: After a hip replacement, most people go home within a few days and recover over several weeks. If you are frail, plan ahead: get equipment fitted, follow your exercise plan, take pain relief so you can move, and get help with daily tasks. Contact your team urgently about signs of infection, a blood clot or dislocation.

content:
A hip replacement can greatly reduce pain and improve mobility, but the first weeks at home can be hard, especially if you are frail. Planning ahead and knowing what to expect can make recovery safer.

This guide covers preparing your home, exercise, pain relief, warning signs and support. It is educational information. Always follow the advice of your surgical team, as instructions vary between hospitals.

Before you go into hospital

  • Ask whether your hospital runs a joint school or pre-operative class.
  • An occupational therapist may assess your home and arrange equipment, such as a raised toilet seat, chair raisers or a perching stool.
  • Move everyday items to waist height and clear trip hazards.
  • Arrange help with shopping, meals and housework for the first few weeks.

The first weeks at home

  • Do the exercises your physiotherapist gave you, little and often.
  • Walk short distances regularly, using your walking aid as advised.
  • Follow any movement precautions your team gives you. These vary between hospitals and operations.
  • Take pain relief as prescribed, so you can move and exercise.
  • Wear compression stockings and take any blood-thinning medicine if prescribed.

Recovery when you are frail

Recovery may be slower if you were frail or weak before surgery. Reablement or intermediate care may be offered after discharge to help you regain independence. Eating well, including enough protein, helps healing and muscle strength.

What to expect

The NHS says most people can stop using walking aids and return to normal activities within around 6 weeks, but full recovery can take longer. Ask your team when you can drive, bathe and climb stairs.

When to get help

  • Call 999 for chest pain or sudden breathlessness, which can be a sign of a blood clot in the lung.
  • Contact your surgical team or NHS 111 urgently for a hot, red, swollen or oozing wound, fever, a painful swollen calf, or sudden severe hip pain with a leg that looks shorter or turned.
  • See your GP if you are not improving as expected or are struggling at home.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Will I need a walking frame?

Many people use a frame or crutches at first and move to sticks as they recover. Your physiotherapist will advise.

What if I live alone?

Tell your team before surgery. You may be offered reablement or intermediate care, and a community alarm can help you feel safer.

Is it normal to feel tired?

Yes. Tiredness is common for several weeks. Pace your activities and rest between them.
